system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker LOSS_MTAP (loss of MTAP expression, usually by 9p21 co-deletion with CDKN2A).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

input.query: MTAP AND (PRMT5 OR WDR77 OR MAT2A) AND (synthetic lethal* OR dependency)

content.thinking: I'm weighing whether to register PRMT5 or WDR77 first. WDR77 looks strongest on the data, but PRMT5 is the druggable, clinically validated target, with WDR77 as its partner, so I'll register both.

input.mechanism: MTAP loss causes MTA accumulation, which partially inhibits PRMT5 by competing with SAM; residual PRMT5 activity becomes limiting, so further PRMT5 depletion is selectively lethal (exploited by MTA-cooperative inhibitors such as MRTX1719).
WDR77 (MEP50) is the obligate cofactor of PRMT5 in the methylosome; with PRMT5 partially inhibited by MTA in MTAP-null cells, loss of WDR77 collapses remaining PRMT5 activity.

input.summary: For MTAP-loss lines, the most selective dependencies were the PRMT5 methylosome (WDR77 and PRMT5), followed by METTL16 and MAT2A. PELO/HBS1L also scored, probably because FOCAD is deleted along with MTAP. Both registered hypotheses replicated in held-out Broad lines and in Sanger screens. PRMT5 is listed first as the best therapeutic target: it is the drug target and is already validated in the clinic with MTA-cooperative inhibitors. WDR77, its obligate partner, has the largest statistical effect (stronger t in every split). Caveats: both genes are broadly essential (about 97–98% of non-MTAP-loss lines are also strongly dependent), so the CRISPR difference is moderate (−0.25 to −0.56). A therapeutic window depends on MTA-cooperative chemistry, not on knockout selectivity alone. Both findings are well established, not new.

findings.claim: Cell lines that have lost MTAP depend more on PRMT5 than other lines (discovery t=-6.1; held-out Broad p=4e-6; Sanger p=9e-13), which supports MTA-cooperative PRMT5 inhibitors for 9p21/MTAP-deleted cancers.
Cell lines that have lost MTAP depend more on WDR77 (MEP50), PRMT5's obligate cofactor; this is the strongest statistical signal (discovery t=-8.2; held-out Broad p=1e-8; Sanger p=4e-15).
